guide.hajj.intro.0: Hajj, the major pilgrimage, is an obligation once in a lifetime for every Muslim who is able to make the journey (Quran 3:97). It takes place in the month of Dhu al-Hijjah, and most of its rites are outside Masjid al-Haram — in Mina, Arafat and Muzdalifah.
guide.hajj.intro.1: Its pillars are ihram, standing at Arafat, Tawaf al-Ifadah, and sa’i (Ministry of Hajj and Umrah).
guide.hajj.intro.2: There are three ways of performing Hajj — tamattu’, qiran and ifrad — which differ slightly (Ministry of Hajj and Umrah). This guide follows tamattu’: Umrah first, during the months of Hajj, then Hajj itself, with a sacrifice (Quran 2:196).
guide.hajj.step.arafah.points.0: Pilgrims pray Dhuhr and Asr together at the time of Dhuhr (Sahih Muslim 1218).
guide.hajj.step.arafah.points.1: The Prophet ﷺ remained standing at Arafat until the sun had set (Sahih Muslim 1218).
guide.hajj.step.arafah.points.2: The Day of Arafah is known for supplication; the best supplication is that of this day (Ministry of Hajj and Umrah).
guide.hajj.step.arafah.summary: Go to Arafat and stand there in remembrance and supplication until sunset. Standing at Arafat is a pillar of Hajj; the Prophet ﷺ said, “Hajj is Arafah.”
guide.hajj.step.arafah.title: The Day of Arafah
guide.hajj.step.ifadah.points.0: “…and let them perform tawaf around the ancient House” (Quran 22:29).
guide.hajj.step.ifadah.points.1: Start in line with the corner of the Black Stone, with the Kaaba on your left, and walk anticlockwise around it. Each circuit ends back at that corner; seven circuits make one tawaf.
guide.hajj.step.ifadah.points.2: At the Black Stone, touch or kiss it if you can reach it. If the crowd does not allow it, face it and point towards it, as the Prophet ﷺ did when he performed tawaf riding a camel (Sahih al-Bukhari 1612).
guide.hajj.step.ifadah.points.3: The Prophet ﷺ performed this tawaf on the Day of Sacrifice, and then drank Zamzam water (Sahih Muslim 1218).
guide.hajj.step.ifadah.summary: Return to Masjid al-Haram for Tawaf al-Ifadah, a pillar of Hajj, then perform sa’i between Safa and Marwah.
guide.hajj.step.ifadah.title: Tawaf al-Ifadah and sa’i
guide.hajj.step.muzdalifah.points.0: After praying Fajr, remember Allah at al-Mash’ar al-Haram until it is light (Quran 2:198; Sahih Muslim 1218).
guide.hajj.step.muzdalifah.points.1: Pilgrims gather pebbles here for the stoning.
guide.hajj.step.muzdalifah.summary: After sunset, go to Muzdalifah, pray Maghrib and Isha together, and spend the night there.
guide.hajj.step.muzdalifah.title: The night at Muzdalifah
guide.hajj.step.nahr.points.0: Throw seven pebbles at Jamrat al-Aqaba, saying “Allahu akbar” with each (Sahih Muslim 1218).
guide.hajj.step.nahr.points.1: Offer the sacrifice required of a pilgrim performing tamattu’ (Quran 2:196).
guide.hajj.step.nahr.points.2: Men shave their heads or shorten their hair; women shorten theirs (Sunan Abi Dawud 1984).
guide.hajj.step.nahr.summary: Stone Jamrat al-Aqaba, offer the sacrifice, and shave or shorten the hair.
guide.hajj.step.nahr.title: The Day of Sacrifice
guide.hajj.step.tarwiyah.points.0: On the 8th, pilgrims put on ihram again and confirm their intention for Hajj.
guide.hajj.step.tarwiyah.points.1: The Prophet ﷺ went to Mina on this day and prayed Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib and Isha there, and Fajr the next morning (Sahih Muslim 1218).
guide.hajj.step.tarwiyah.recitation: Here I am, O Allah, here I am. Here I am; You have no partner; here I am. All praise and blessings are Yours, and all sovereignty. You have no partner.
guide.hajj.step.tarwiyah.summary: Enter ihram for Hajj from where you are staying in Makkah, and go to Mina.
guide.hajj.step.tarwiyah.title: The Day of Tarwiyah: to Mina
guide.hajj.step.tashreeq.points.0: Begin with the small jamrah, then the middle one, then Jamrat al-Aqaba, saying “Allahu akbar” with each pebble, and pausing to supplicate after the first two (Sahih al-Bukhari 1751).
guide.hajj.step.tashreeq.points.1: Pilgrims may leave Mina on the 12th, before sunset, or stay for the 13th (Quran 2:203).
guide.hajj.step.tashreeq.summary: Spend the nights in Mina, and each day after midday throw seven pebbles at each of the three jamarat.
guide.hajj.step.tashreeq.title: The Days of Tashreeq: stoning in Mina
guide.hajj.step.umrah-first.points.0: The Umrah guide explains each of its steps.
guide.hajj.step.umrah-first.summary: In Hajj tamattu’, the pilgrim first performs Umrah and then leaves ihram until the days of Hajj (Quran 2:196).
guide.hajj.step.umrah-first.title: Perform Umrah
guide.hajj.step.wada.points.0: Start in line with the corner of the Black Stone, with the Kaaba on your left, and walk anticlockwise around it. Each circuit ends back at that corner; seven circuits make one tawaf.
guide.hajj.step.wada.points.1: At the Black Stone, touch or kiss it if you can reach it. If the crowd does not allow it, face it and point towards it, as the Prophet ﷺ did when he performed tawaf riding a camel (Sahih al-Bukhari 1612).
guide.hajj.step.wada.summary: Before leaving Makkah, perform the farewell tawaf (Tawaf al-Wada’), so that the last act is at the House. Women who are menstruating are excused (Sahih al-Bukhari 1755).
guide.hajj.step.wada.title: The farewell tawaf
guide.hajj.summary: The days of Hajj, from the 8th to the 13th of Dhu al-Hijjah, step by step.
guide.hajj.title: How to perform Hajj
guide.umrah.intro.0: Umrah, the “lesser pilgrimage”, can be performed at any time of the year. Its rites are entering ihram, tawaf around the Kaaba, sa’i between Safa and Marwah, and shaving or shortening the hair.
guide.umrah.step.enter.points.0: The Mataf is the open, marble-paved area around the Kaaba where tawaf is performed.
guide.umrah.step.enter.summary: Enter the mosque through any of its gates and make your way to the Mataf around the Kaaba.
guide.umrah.step.enter.title: Enter Masjid al-Haram
guide.umrah.step.hair.points.0: The Quran mentions pilgrims with “heads shaved and hair shortened” (Quran 48:27).
guide.umrah.step.hair.points.1: Women do not shave; they only shorten the hair (Sunan Abi Dawud 1984).
guide.umrah.step.hair.points.2: With this, Umrah is complete and the restrictions of ihram end.
guide.umrah.step.hair.summary: Men shave their heads or shorten their hair; women shorten theirs slightly. This completes Umrah.
guide.umrah.step.hair.title: Shave or shorten the hair
guide.umrah.step.ihram.points.0: Bathe before entering ihram: the Prophet ﷺ told even a woman who had just given birth to do so (Sahih Muslim 1218).
guide.umrah.step.ihram.points.1: Men wear two white, unsewn cloths. They do not wear shirts, turbans, trousers, hooded cloaks, or footwear that covers the ankles (Sahih al-Bukhari 1542).
guide.umrah.step.ihram.points.2: Women wear their ordinary modest clothing, but do not cover the face with a niqab or wear gloves (Sahih al-Bukhari 1838).
guide.umrah.step.ihram.points.3: Make the intention for Umrah and begin reciting the talbiyah.
guide.umrah.step.ihram.points.4: While in ihram, avoid perfume (Sahih al-Bukhari 1542), cutting the hair (Quran 2:196), hunting (Quran 5:95) and marital relations (Quran 2:197).
guide.umrah.step.ihram.recitation: Here I am, O Allah, here I am. Here I am; You have no partner; here I am. All praise and blessings are Yours, and all sovereignty. You have no partner.
guide.umrah.step.ihram.summary: Before passing the miqat — the stations around Makkah set by the Prophet ﷺ — enter the state of ihram.
guide.umrah.step.ihram.title: Enter ihram
guide.umrah.step.ihram.where: At the miqat, before reaching Makkah
guide.umrah.step.maqam.points.0: The Quran tells the believers to take the standing place of Ibrahim as a place of prayer (Quran 2:125). After his tawaf the Prophet ﷺ went to it, recited this verse and prayed two units (Sahih Muslim 1218).
guide.umrah.step.maqam.summary: After tawaf, pray two units of prayer (rak’ahs) behind Maqam Ibrahim where space allows.
guide.umrah.step.maqam.title: Pray two units behind Maqam Ibrahim
guide.umrah.step.sai.points.0: On reaching Safa, the Prophet ﷺ recited “Indeed, Safa and Marwah are among the symbols of Allah” (Quran 2:158), climbed it until he could see the Kaaba, faced it, and declared the oneness and greatness of Allah. He did the same on Marwah (Sahih Muslim 1218).
guide.umrah.step.sai.points.1: Between the two green markers, men who are able walk at a brisk pace (Ministry of Hajj and Umrah).
guide.umrah.step.sai.summary: Walk between Safa and Marwah seven times, starting at Safa and ending at Marwah. Going from Safa to Marwah is one lap, and coming back is another.
guide.umrah.step.sai.title: Sa’i between Safa and Marwah
guide.umrah.step.tawaf.points.0: Start in line with the corner of the Black Stone, with the Kaaba on your left, and walk anticlockwise around it. Each circuit ends back at that corner; seven circuits make one tawaf.
guide.umrah.step.tawaf.points.1: At the Black Stone, touch or kiss it if you can reach it. If the crowd does not allow it, face it and point towards it, as the Prophet ﷺ did when he performed tawaf riding a camel (Sahih al-Bukhari 1612).
guide.umrah.step.tawaf.points.2: Touch the Yemeni Corner if you can (Sahih al-Bukhari 1609).
guide.umrah.step.tawaf.points.3: Walk around the outside of Hijr Ismail, which is part of the House (Sahih al-Bukhari 1584).
guide.umrah.step.tawaf.points.4: Spend the circuits in remembrance of Allah, recitation and supplication.
guide.umrah.step.tawaf.points.5: In the tawaf on arrival, men walk briskly in the first three circuits and normally in the other four (Sahih Muslim 1218).
guide.umrah.step.tawaf.summary: Walk around the Kaaba seven times, anticlockwise, beginning and ending at the corner of the Black Stone.
guide.umrah.step.tawaf.title: Tawaf
guide.umrah.step.zamzam.points.0: The Prophet ﷺ drank Zamzam water during his Hajj (Sahih Muslim 1218).
guide.umrah.step.zamzam.summary: Zamzam water is provided throughout the mosque.
guide.umrah.step.zamzam.title: Drink Zamzam water
guide.umrah.summary: Ihram, tawaf, prayer at Maqam Ibrahim, sa’i, and shaving or shortening the hair.
guide.umrah.title: How to perform Umrah
place.babAlSalam.description.0: Bab al-Salam — the Gate of Peace — is one of the historic gates of the mosque. It lies along the Mas'a, between Safa and Marwah but closer to Marwah, and gives access to the Mas'a.
place.babAlSalam.modelNote: Its position is as mapped in OpenStreetMap; its architecture is simplified.
place.babAlSalam.name: Bab al-Salam
place.babAlSalam.summary: The Gate of Peace, along the Mas'a near Marwah.
place.babAlTawbah.description.0: Bab al-Tawbah, the Door of Repentance, is a golden door on the right as one enters. It opens onto an enclosed staircase leading to a hatch in the roof.
place.babAlTawbah.modelNote: The staircase is shown closed, as an enclosure in the corner. Its size, and the door’s decoration, drawn in the style of the Kaaba’s outer door, are approximate.
place.babAlTawbah.name: Bab al-Tawbah
place.babAlTawbah.summary: The golden door on the right as one enters, to the stairs up to the roof.
place.babAlUmrah.description.0: Bab al-Umrah is on the north-western side of the mosque and gives direct access towards the Mataf. It was renovated as part of the King Abdullah expansion.
place.babAlUmrah.modelNote: Its position is as mapped in OpenStreetMap; its architecture is simplified.
place.babAlUmrah.name: Bab al-Umrah
place.babAlUmrah.summary: A gate on the north-western side, leading towards the Mataf.
place.blackStone.description.0: The Black Stone is set into the eastern corner of the Kaaba, about one and a half metres above the ground, and is held in a silver frame.
place.blackStone.description.1: Each circuit of tawaf begins and ends at this corner. Pilgrims kiss or touch the stone when they are able to, following the practice of the Prophet ﷺ.
place.blackStone.description.2: Umar ibn al-Khattab is reported to have said, before kissing it, that he knew it was only a stone that could neither benefit nor harm, and that he kissed it only because he had seen the Prophet ﷺ do so (Sahih al-Bukhari 1597).
place.blackStone.name: Black Stone
place.blackStone.summary: The stone set in the eastern corner of the Kaaba, where tawaf begins and ends.
place.clockTower.description.0: The Makkah Royal Clock Tower is part of the Abraj Al-Bait complex, which stands just south of Masjid al-Haram, outside the mosque. Completed in 2012, it is about 601 metres tall.
place.clockTower.description.1: Each of its four clock faces is 43 metres across. By day the faces are white with black hands; at night they are lit green with white hands. The Saudi coat of arms is at the centre of each face, behind the hands. Above the faces, “Allahu akbar” (God is the greatest) is written on the north and south sides, and the Shahada (“There is no god but Allah; Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah”) on the east and west sides. The clock keeps Arabia Standard Time (UTC+3).
place.clockTower.description.2: The top floors of the clock tower house the Clock Tower Museum, and there is an observation deck higher up, at about 484 metres, at the base of the spire. Visitors look out over Masjid al-Haram from far above.
place.clockTower.modelNote: The tower stands where it is mapped (OpenStreetMap), as a simplified outline. Its clock faces show the current time in Makkah and follow the day and night colours; the dial’s markings, hands and emblem are a simplified drawing, not the real artwork. Zoom in to read them. “View from the balcony” takes you up to a viewing balcony beneath the north clock face, about 370 metres up; its position and size are approximate, and the mosque below is the same simplified model.
place.clockTower.name: Makkah Royal Clock Tower
place.clockTower.summary: The tall clock tower of the Abraj Al-Bait complex, outside the mosque.
place.greenMarkers.description.0: Green lights mark a section of the Mas'a. Between the two green markers, men who are able are encouraged to move at a brisk pace, following the example of the Prophet ﷺ; others continue at a normal walk.
place.greenMarkers.description.1: The narration in Sahih al-Bukhari describes Hajar running when she came down into the valley between the two hills (Sahih al-Bukhari 3364).
place.greenMarkers.modelNote: The position and length of the green-lit section are approximate.
place.greenMarkers.name: Green markers
place.greenMarkers.summary: Green lights marking a section of the Mas'a.
place.hijrIsmail.description.0: Hijr Ismail, also known as al-Hatim, is the area enclosed by the low, semicircular wall beside the north-western side of the Kaaba.
place.hijrIsmail.description.1: Aisha asked the Prophet ﷺ whether this area was part of the Kaaba, and he said that it was: it had been left outside the walls because the Quraysh did not have enough funds when they rebuilt the Kaaba (Sahih al-Bukhari 1584). Tawaf is therefore performed around the outside of the Hijr.
place.hijrIsmail.modelNote: The wall’s curve, height and thickness are approximate.
place.hijrIsmail.name: Hijr Ismail
place.hijrIsmail.summary: The low semicircular wall beside the north-western side of the Kaaba.
place.kaaba.description.0: The Kaaba is the cube-shaped building at the centre of Masjid al-Haram in Makkah and the most sacred site in Islam. Muslims everywhere face towards it in prayer; this direction is called the qibla (Quran 2:144).
place.kaaba.description.1: The Quran describes it as the first House of worship established for mankind (Quran 3:96) and tells how Ibrahim (Abraham) and Ismail (Ishmael) raised its foundations (Quran 2:127).
place.kaaba.description.2: During Hajj and Umrah, pilgrims perform tawaf around the Kaaba (Quran 22:29): seven circuits, walked anticlockwise so that the Kaaba stays on the left.
place.kaaba.modelNote: Modelled with approximate published dimensions. Surface details are simplified.
place.kaaba.name: Kaaba
place.kaaba.summary: The House at the centre of Masjid al-Haram, which Muslims face in prayer.
place.kaabaDoor.description.0: The door of the Kaaba is on its north-eastern wall, close to the corner of the Black Stone, and is set about two metres above the ground.
place.kaabaDoor.description.1: A richly embroidered curtain, the sitara, hangs over the door. It is the most elaborately decorated part of the kiswah.
place.kaabaDoor.description.2: In a narration in Sahih al-Bukhari, Aisha asked why the door was set so high. The Prophet ﷺ explained that her people, the Quraysh, had built it that way so that they could let in or keep out whomever they wished (Sahih al-Bukhari 1584).
place.kaabaDoor.modelNote: The door is shown behind its curtain, using a 2016 photograph of the real curtain; the golden door shows through its opening as in the photograph.
place.kaabaDoor.name: Door of the Kaaba
place.kaabaDoor.summary: The raised door on the north-eastern wall, behind its embroidered curtain.
place.kaabaInterior.description.0: The door opens onto a single room whose floor is about two metres above the ground where tawaf is performed. The floor is of marble and limestone, and the walls are clad in pale marble halfway to the roof, with dark green marble along the floor and in bands.
place.kaabaInterior.description.1: Above the marble, the upper walls and the ceiling are covered with a green cloth. Old lamps of silver and gold hang close together from rods between the pillars. Plaques recording those who renovated the Kaaba are set in the walls: nine, all in thuluth script except one in kufic, and a tenth added in the time of King Fahd.
place.kaabaInterior.description.2: The Prophet ﷺ entered the Kaaba and prayed inside it. Bilal, who was with him, later told Ibn Umar where he had prayed: between the two pillars on the left as one enters (Sahih al-Bukhari 397).
place.kaabaInterior.description.3: The Kaaba is opened only on a few occasions, such as the ceremony of washing it, and its keys are held by the Banu Shaybah. The Prophet ﷺ told Aisha, who wished to pray inside, to pray in the Hijr, for it is part of the House (Sunan Abi Dawud 2028).
place.kaabaInterior.modelNote: Visitors cannot normally go inside; this view is for learning. It is drawn after published photographs of the room, but its measurements are not published, so it is fitted within the outer walls with an approximate ceiling height. The number and places of the lamps and plaques, the plaques’ carving and the cloth’s pattern are illustrative, not copies of the real ones.
place.kaabaInterior.name: Inside the Kaaba
place.kaabaInterior.summary: A single room, its floor about two metres above the Mataf, opened only on a few occasions.
place.kaabaPillars.description.0: Three pillars of wood, banded with gilded metal, stand inside the Kaaba and hold up its roof. Between one of them and the other two stands a small white cupboard where perfume is kept.
place.kaabaPillars.description.1: Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr set up the three pillars when he rebuilt the Kaaba. They were replaced during the renovation in the time of King Fahd.
place.kaabaPillars.description.2: In the Prophet’s time the roof stood on six pillars: when he prayed inside, he had one pillar on his left, one on his right and three behind him (Sahih al-Bukhari 505).
place.kaabaPillars.modelNote: The pillars are drawn as photographed, in a row; their spacing and the cupboard’s place are approximate.
place.kaabaPillars.name: The pillars inside the Kaaba
place.kaabaPillars.summary: Three pillars that hold up the roof, first set there by Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr.
place.kingAbdulazizGate.description.0: King Abdulaziz Gate (Gate 1) is one of the principal entrances of Masjid al-Haram. It is on the southern side of the mosque, opposite Ajyad Street, near the Abraj Al-Bait complex.
place.kingAbdulazizGate.modelNote: Its position is as mapped in OpenStreetMap; its architecture is simplified.
place.kingAbdulazizGate.name: King Abdulaziz Gate
place.kingAbdulazizGate.summary: Gate 1, a principal entrance on the southern side.
place.kingAbdullahGate.description.0: King Abdullah Gate (Gate 100) is the central entrance to the King Abdullah expansion, on the northern side of the mosque. It is a triple-arched gate flanked by two minarets.
place.kingAbdullahGate.modelNote: Its position is as mapped in OpenStreetMap. The King Abdullah expansion is shown from outside only, and the gate as a single closed arch; its architecture is simplified.
place.kingAbdullahGate.name: King Abdullah Gate
place.kingAbdullahGate.summary: Gate 100, the central entrance of the King Abdullah expansion.
place.kingFahdGate.description.0: King Fahd Gate (Gate 79) is one of the principal gates of Masjid al-Haram. It leads into the wing added in the second Saudi expansion, under King Fahd, on the western side of the mosque. The gate has three portals and is flanked by two minarets.
place.kingFahdGate.modelNote: Its position is as mapped in OpenStreetMap; it is shown as a single arch and its architecture is simplified.
place.kingFahdGate.name: King Fahd Gate
place.kingFahdGate.summary: Gate 79, the entrance to the King Fahd wing, on the western side.
place.kiswah.description.0: The kiswah is the black silk cloth that covers the Kaaba. Inscriptions, including the Shahada, are woven into the silk itself, black on black. Verses of the Quran are embroidered on it in gold and silver thread, including a broad band that runs around the Kaaba about two-thirds of the way up.
place.kiswah.description.1: The band is made of four embroidered pieces on each side. Below it, square panels with circular medallions mark the four corners, and the most elaborately decorated part, a curtain called the sitara, hangs over the door.
place.kiswah.description.2: A new kiswah is made and placed on the Kaaba each year.
place.kiswah.modelNote: The cloth, the door curtain and the band are shown with photographs of real kiswah: the woven calligraphy from a photograph of a kiswah fragment in a museum, the curtain from a 2016 photograph, and the band from photographs of two historical band panels (Khalili Collection) and the modern dedication panel. Because only three band panels are available, they repeat, and the verses do not appear in their true order. The corner panels are represented by abstract designs.
place.kiswah.name: Kiswah
place.kiswah.summary: The black, embroidered cloth that covers the Kaaba.
place.maqamIbrahim.description.0: Maqam Ibrahim — the Station of Ibrahim — is a stone associated with the Prophet Ibrahim (Abraham). It is kept in a glass and metal enclosure on the north-eastern side of the Kaaba, facing its door. The stone bears impressions traditionally identified as his footprints.
place.maqamIbrahim.description.1: According to a narration in Sahih al-Bukhari, Ibrahim stood on a stone while raising the walls of the House, as Ismail handed him the building stones (Sahih al-Bukhari 3364).
place.maqamIbrahim.description.2: The Quran mentions the standing place of Ibrahim among the clear signs at the House (Quran 3:97) and tells the believers to take it as a place of prayer (Quran 2:125). After his tawaf, the Prophet ﷺ went to the Maqam, recited this verse and prayed two units of prayer (Sahih Muslim 1218); pilgrims follow this practice where space allows.
place.maqamIbrahim.modelNote: The enclosure’s shape and its distance from the Kaaba are approximate.
place.maqamIbrahim.name: Maqam Ibrahim
place.maqamIbrahim.summary: The Station of Ibrahim, a stone kept in an enclosure near the Kaaba.
place.marwah.description.0: Marwah is the hill at the northern end of the Mas'a, where sa'i ends after the seventh lap.
place.marwah.description.1: According to the narration in Sahih al-Bukhari, it was when Hajar reached Marwah on her last lap that she heard a voice and then found the water of Zamzam (Sahih al-Bukhari 3364).
place.marwah.modelNote: The rock and the dome above it are simplified.
place.marwah.name: Marwah
place.masa.description.0: The Mas'a is the long gallery between the hills of Safa and Marwah. Here pilgrims perform sa'i: walking between the two hills seven times, beginning at Safa and ending at Marwah.
place.masa.description.1: The rite recalls Hajar, who went back and forth between the two hills searching for water for her son Ismail; the Prophet ﷺ said that this is the origin of the people's sa'i between them (Sahih al-Bukhari 3364). The Quran names Safa and Marwah among the symbols of Allah (Quran 2:158).
place.masa.modelNote: Only the ground floor is shown. Its outline and the positions of Safa and Marwah follow OpenStreetMap; the interior is simplified.
place.masa.name: Mas'a
place.masa.summary: The gallery between Safa and Marwah, where pilgrims perform sa'i.
place.mataf.description.0: The Mataf is the open, marble-paved area surrounding the Kaaba, where pilgrims perform tawaf.
place.mataf.description.1: Tawaf consists of seven circuits around the Kaaba, beginning and ending at the corner of the Black Stone, with the Kaaba kept on the left.
place.mataf.description.2: The Mataf has been enlarged in successive expansions of the mosque.
place.mataf.modelNote: Only the ground level is shown; the open area’s outline follows OpenStreetMap.
place.mataf.name: Mataf
place.mataf.summary: The open, marble-paved area around the Kaaba where tawaf is performed.
place.mizab.description.0: The Mizab is the golden rainwater spout on the roof of the Kaaba. It projects from the north-western side, above Hijr Ismail, and carries rainwater off the roof into that area.
place.mizab.name: Mizab al-Rahmah
place.mizab.summary: The golden rainwater spout on the roof of the Kaaba.
place.ottomanPortico.description.0: The arcades crowned with rows of small domes that surround the open courtyard are known as the Ottoman porticoes. They are among the oldest surviving parts of the mosque’s structure.
place.ottomanPortico.description.1: They date from the Ottoman period, beginning with a renovation of the mosque in the sixteenth century, and were preserved and restored during the modern expansions.
place.ottomanPortico.modelNote: Their plan follows OpenStreetMap: they run around the north, west and south sides of the courtyard, which on the east side reaches the halls. The arcades, columns and domes are simplified.
place.ottomanPortico.name: Ottoman porticoes
place.ottomanPortico.summary: The domed arcades around the courtyard, among the oldest parts of the building.
place.safa.description.0: Safa is the small hill at the southern end of the Mas'a, where sa'i begins. Part of its rock remains visible within the building.
place.safa.description.1: The Quran mentions Safa and Marwah together among the symbols of Allah (Quran 2:158). The Prophet ﷺ began his sa'i at Safa, reciting this verse (Sahih Muslim 1218).
place.safa.modelNote: The rock and the dome above it are simplified.
place.safa.name: Safa
place.yemeniCorner.description.0: The Yemeni Corner is the southern corner of the Kaaba, named for the direction it faces.
place.yemeniCorner.description.1: Abdullah ibn Umar reported that he saw the Prophet ﷺ touch only the two Yemeni corners — this one and the corner of the Black Stone (Sahih al-Bukhari 1609).
place.yemeniCorner.name: Yemeni Corner
place.yemeniCorner.summary: The southern corner of the Kaaba, facing towards Yemen.
place.zamzam.description.0: The Zamzam well lies within Masjid al-Haram, a short distance east of the Kaaba. According to a narration in Sahih al-Bukhari, its water emerged for Hajar (Hagar) and her infant son Ismail after she had searched for water between Safa and Marwah (Sahih al-Bukhari 3364).
place.zamzam.description.1: The well lies beneath the Mataf, about 21 metres east of the Kaaba on the side of Maqam Ibrahim, in line with the Multazam. It is not visible today: in the 1960s its opening was lowered into a basement beneath the Mataf, and in 2003 the basement entrances were closed and the marking on the floor above the well was removed. Zamzam water is provided for visitors throughout the mosque.
place.zamzam.modelNote: The circle on the floor, lettered “بئر زمزم” (the Zamzam well), is drawn for this model to show the well’s approximate location. There is no such marking on the Mataf today, and nothing of the well itself is modelled.
place.zamzam.name: Zamzam Well
place.zamzam.summary: The well within the mosque, a short distance east of the Kaaba.

ui.app.tagline: An educational, approximate 3D representation of the Sacred Mosque in Makkah.
ui.app.title: Masjid al-Haram 3D Explorer

ui.guide.chooserIntro: Step-by-step guides to the rites. Steps inside Masjid al-Haram are shown in the 3D view; you can follow the tawaf and sa’i routes on foot.
ui.guide.disclaimer: This is a simplified overview for orientation, not a religious ruling. Details differ between the schools of Islamic law, and the authorities in Makkah set the practical arrangements each year. Follow the guidance of qualified scholars and the official instructions.
ui.guide.heading: Hajj and Umrah guide
ui.guide.outside: This step takes place outside Masjid al-Haram, so it is not shown in the 3D view.
ui.guide.routeSai: In the 3D view, the gold line marks the route between Safa and Marwah, the arrows the way there and back, and the green strip the section between the green markers. The walk goes there and back seven times, ending at Marwah, and hastens between the green markers as men do; any movement key or the joystick stops it. These are guide markings, not part of the mosque.
ui.guide.routeTawaf: In the 3D view, the gold circle marks the tawaf route, the arrows its direction, and the green line the starting point in line with the Black Stone. These are guide markings, not part of the mosque.
ui.help.about: This is a simplified, approximate 3D representation of Masjid al-Haram made for learning. It is not an exact architectural model: the Kaaba and the features around it follow published approximate dimensions, while the wider mosque is schematic and compressed in size. Only the ground level can be explored.
ui.help.accuracy: Descriptions are written from the sources listed with each place. Each panel also notes what is approximate in the model.
ui.help.creditsBody: The 3D model and most textures were generated in code for Qurany Piroz. The kiswah photographs are by the people and collections below, used under their licences (cropped, scaled and combined). Rendering uses three.js (MIT licence).
ui.help.heading: About this explorer
ui.help.night: Night view is an artistic impression of the floodlit mosque, not an exact record of its lighting.

ui.toast.balcony: On the clock tower’s balcony, about 370 m up. Walk along it, zoom in, or choose “Back down”.
